description: We are orbit Guardians, a team of passionate engineering students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
summary:
MarsPath, developed by Team Orbit Guardians, is a Mars exploration planning and simulation prototype for future human explorers. It combines satellite observations and rover-derived data to connect scientific destinations with terrain-aware route planning.

The platform supports terrain and past-habitability exploration in Jezero Crater and water-ice evidence comparison in Arcadia Planitia. It integrates orbital imagery, elevation and slope, SWIM ice evidence and historical NASA MEDA environmental observations.

Users can select destinations, compare routes using A* pathfinding, plan return journeys and record observations. Simulated compass and visor guidance, route-deviation warnings and illustrative resource estimates help users rehearse an exploration mission.

MarsPath addresses the challenge by bringing scientific evidence and navigation into one workflow while distinguishing observations, models and simulation.

Our proposed next stage is an offline, voice-assisted intelligent system on embedded hardware, reducing manual interaction and dependence on connectivity. We also plan to investigate ML estimates beyond rover coverage, with independent validation and uncertainty reporting.

MarsPath aims to make scientific information accessible during exploration while considering limited power and computing resources. It remains a research prototype, not an operational navigation or life-support system.

MarsPath project documentation

Navigation and scientific exploration for future Marswalks

Team Orbit Guardians
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
15 November 2026

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 1. MarsPath home screen supplied by the team. Website illustrations are interface artwork, not evidence of an observed mission.

Purpose and scope

MarsPath connects scientific destinations with terrain-aware route planning, simulated navigation and recorded observations. This document explains the current prototype, its data and algorithms, and the proposed transition to an offline voice-assisted intelligent exploration system.

The intended readers are competition judges, scientific collaborators and developers. The current system is a research and simulation prototype. It does not provide operational astronaut navigation, live Mars positioning or validated life-support advice.

Documentation baseline: LAST_MarsPath_7_05.zip, whose internal project folder is LAST_MarsPath_5_35, together with the team’s website screenshots supplied in img.zip. Screenshots are treated as captured interface evidence; they do not establish the exact code revision running at capture time.

1 Project overview

Abstract

MarsPath is a Mars surface-exploration planning and simulation prototype developed by Team Orbit Guardians. It combines satellite observations and rover-derived information to help future explorers understand both where to travel and why a location matters scientifically. The current missions cover local terrain exploration in Jezero Crater, regional past-habitability investigation in Jezero and water-ice candidate comparison in Arcadia Planitia. The platform presents imagery, elevation and slope, subsurface-ice evidence and historical rover environmental observations with their limitations.

A custom A* planner compares route objectives on supplied terrain grids. Users can choose destinations, consider a modeled return journey, rehearse movement using compass or visor guidance and record observations in a saved session. The proposed next stage is a locally operated, voice-assisted intelligent system on embedded hardware. Machine-learning estimates beyond rover coverage are a research direction requiring independent validation and uncertainty reporting. The project’s contribution is the connection between scientific context, route decisions and observation records, while keeping observations, models and simulation distinguishable.

The challenge and intended use

A surface excursion needs more than a broad planetary map. An explorer needs a scientific objective, local terrain context, a route and a way to document findings. MarsPath addresses this decision sequence using the supplied study areas. It does not claim global route coverage or transfer local rover measurements to arbitrary locations.

What makes MarsPath distinctive

MarsPath connects “Where should we explore?” with “How could we get there?” It brings satellite imagery, rover-derived records and scientific evidence into one workflow for investigating terrain, potential subsurface water ice and past habitability. Users can compare candidate locations, plan terrain-aware routes where suitable data exists, practise a simulated Marswalk and record observations in saved exploration sessions. Crucially, MarsPath distinguishes measured data, calculated results and simulations, highlighting unverified locations and coverage limits rather than presenting every destination as equally understood.

Document guide

2 Mission scope and user workflow

Figure 2. Mission selection presents terrain, water-ice and past-habitability exploration as distinct scientific choices.

Planning sequence

The user chooses a mission and a destination. In local terrain exploration, a destination can be a candidate, a named model landmark or a traversable map point. The start can use the model landing reference or a user-selected position within supported coverage. Advanced row and column inputs refer to local grid cells, not latitude and longitude. Candidate zones are areas represented by planning points; selecting a point does not certify the whole polygon as traversable.

After examining the evidence, the user generates and compares routes. Optional science time, nearby stops and a return reserve are planning inputs. Simulation provides a rehearsal of the selected route. The summary then supports reviewing the journey and entering observations. The current note-entry interface is shown after navigation; the reviewed source does not establish the same visible note-entry flow for the science-only Arcadia path.

 

3 Data sources and processing

MarsPath uses team-supplied processed files. An instrument or project identification is not a substitute for the original product ID, acquisition date and processing history. The following register distinguishes documented application processing from upstream GIS work that still needs confirmation. [S1–S5]

Interpretation of environmental and ice data

ATS observations describe historical air temperature at the rover. TIRS summaries describe infrared irradiance in W/m², not ground temperature. The current demonstration can select a historical Mars hour using the device’s same-numbered local hour; Earth local time is not Mars local mean solar time. The Sol 15 record is not a route-wide heat map or a current weather feed.

SWIM consistency scores are evidence related to possible subsurface ice. They are not confirmed ice deposits, water volumes or astronaut hazard probabilities. These data categories also do not establish three independently measured, co-registered layers at every route point. The previously proposed but undownloaded HiRISE mosaic is not credited as a used dataset.

 

4 Coordinate systems and terrain preparation

Spatial reference and resolution

Candidate records use Mars east-positive longitude and north-positive latitude. The local model uses a spherical Mars equirectangular projection, documented as consistent with ESRI:103885, with a model radius of 3,396,190 m. Mars coordinates must not be treated as Earth WGS84 coordinates. Regional routes use their own supplied Mars projection and raster transform. [S2, S3]

The local source elevation and slope rasters are sampled at 1 m. Routing uses nominal 5 m cells on a 401 × 401 grid. A finer image or DEM pixel does not establish equivalent navigation accuracy. The terrain preparation script expects 2001 × 2001 source rasters and preserves unavailable samples at the outer boundary. The relationship between the 2001 m raster extent and the nominal navigation-grid extent requires geotransform validation; source metadata and grid alignment are not yet fully verified.

Preparation pipeline

The supplied prepare_terrain.py script reads GeoTIFF values using OpenCV and NumPy, checks expected dimensions and georeferencing tags, and masks NoData. It creates display previews, sampled terrain values and a subsampled elevation mesh. This is web preparation of an existing DEM and slope raster; it does not demonstrate how the original DEM or slope dataset was produced. Original products, vertical reference, acquisition dates and slope derivation method must come from the GIS team.

The visor mesh is derived from available elevation, with coarse sampling for display. It is not a camera reconstruction of rocks or a verified ground-level photograph. Terrain and model coverage must remain visible when a user moves to a location without elevation support.

Figure 3. Local map planning with an advanced grid destination. The imagery, model grid and selected landmark must retain their distinct accuracy limits.

5 Routing algorithm and planning assumptions

A star search

The local routing engine is a custom Python A* implementation using heapq. It searches eight neighboring cells and ranks candidates by accumulated cost plus an estimated remaining cost. A* suits the existing weighted raster model, accepts blocked cells and needs no training data or cloud inference. Dijkstra supports weighted routes without a goal heuristic; breadth-first search does not directly represent the unequal costs used here. No measured speed or energy advantage over those alternatives is claimed. [S2, R4]

Here g is accumulated path cost and h is octile distance. With row difference dr and column difference dc, the heuristic uses straight steps of 5 m and diagonal steps of 5√2 m. It is a lower bound for the current local objectives because their traversable multipliers are at least one. Optimality is relative to this graph and cost model, not to astronaut safety.

The local slope multiplier is one plus 0.035 times the 1.45 power of max(0, slope − 5). Missing slope receives a multiplier of 1.5. These are project assumptions. Class 255 blocks a cell, and diagonal steps are rejected when either adjoining orthogonal cell is blocked. The displayed “Risk-aware balanced” label must not be interpreted as a validated probability of harm. Balanced scores are not directly comparable with scores that omit the slope multiplier.

Return time and resource model

Return paths are calculated independently. Travel time uses an illustrative 22 m/min speed. Total planned time adds outbound travel, return travel and science time; usable time subtracts the requested reserve from the total budget. Illustrative oxygen and battery use are total minutes multiplied by 0.70 and 0.45 percentage points per minute respectively. These constants are not suit measurements or physiological models. The regional 20 m planner is separate; local balanced-route and resource behaviour should not be assumed identical across every mission.

 

6 Navigation and scientific observations

Guidance and warnings

The navigation screen presents route progress, bearing and distance. Map north provides a reference for bearings; rotating the camera is not equivalent to changing the simulated direction of travel. A heading-offset test supports demonstrating a wrong-direction dialog, acknowledgement and alignment with the route. Position-deviation logic compares a supplied position with the route; the backend corridor check includes an accuracy allowance. These are simulated or manual inputs, not an astronaut location service.

Figure 4. Navigation screen with map view, playback controls and maneuver guidance. This screenshot shows the interface; it does not demonstrate a triggered warning.

The available views include the orbital map, a simulated visor and contextual surface imagery where supplied. A regional photograph should not be presented as the exact view at an arbitrary waypoint. Live heat, radiation or dust alerts require appropriate spatial measurements and validated thresholds; historical MEDA records alone cannot support them.

Observation records

After navigation, users can type observations linked to the session and location. The current component limits notes to 2,000 characters and saves through the backend. Sessions and observations are stored in SQLite; if the API is unavailable, this observation component cannot save or load records. Printing the summary or saving it as PDF supports sharing a report, but does not transmit a scientific discovery to mission control.

Figure 5. Field-observation form. The captured session contains no saved observation; the screenshot demonstrates the entry interface rather than persistence success.

 

7 Worked example from the website

The team supplied a captured Jezero terrain-planning sequence for the model destination labelled Wright Brothers Field on 15 November 2026. The summary identifies grid row 194, column 216 and explicitly describes this as a provisional landmark anchor, not an independently verified field-center coordinate. The results below are transcribed from that interface, not from an independently reproduced experiment. [S6]

Figure 6. Captured timeline: 4.2 minutes outbound, 10 minutes science time and 4.2 minutes return.

The shortest and lower-cost cards show the same rounded distance and cost in this example. The balanced card also shows approximately 92 m and 4.2 minutes. This is a useful demonstration of coincident solutions on an easy corridor, not evidence that the objectives always agree or that one improves on the others. A separate contrasting-terrain example is needed to demonstrate a meaningful trade-off.

 

8 Software architecture and operation

Service interfaces

The local route endpoint is POST /api/routes/generate. POST /api/navigation/deviation checks a supplied position against a route. Sessions use POST /api/sessions, GET and PATCH /api/sessions/{id}, and POST /api/sessions/{id}/observations. Historical MEDA content is served through /api/science/thermal/sol-15 and related temperature endpoints. Regional route handling is a separate module. CORS must permit PATCH as well as GET and POST for session updates. [S2]

Local startup

The supplied README specifies Python 3.10 or later and Node.js 20.19 or later, or 22.12 or later. On Windows, start_all_windows.bat starts the local services. The usual frontend address is http://127.0.0.1:5173; the backend is typically at port 8000, with API documentation at /docs. First installation requires dependencies. If a port is occupied, check for a previously running instance before starting another.

For manual startup, create a Python virtual environment in backend, install requirements.txt and run uvicorn main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000. In frontend, install the package dependencies, configure the local environment if required and run npm run dev. These are development instructions from the project package, not a production deployment certification.

Storage and offline behaviour

Back up the SQLite file before replacing a project folder if historical sessions matter. Do not commit personal session databases, secrets, node_modules or virtual environments to a public repository. Keep dependency manifests, safe example environment files, startup scripts and documentation. Public deployment also needs appropriate access control, transport security and retention decisions; a locally available database is not a complete multi-user security design.

Static candidate and historical thermal fallbacks do not make the whole application offline. Route generation still requires the local backend. Fonts, model-viewer and contextual imagery may use external services. Full offline packaging must include runtime dependencies and required assets and must be tested with networking disabled.

 

9 Reliability beyond rover coverage

Evidence at the target location

Satellite observations can cover places a rover has not visited, but their resolution, age and registration determine what can be inferred. Rover-derived observations provide local context and cannot simply be copied to a distant waypoint. A route is only as reliable as its input terrain, coordinate transformations and model assumptions. A missing layer should remain unavailable rather than being silently replaced by a guessed value.

Proposed machine learning study

No trained or validated ML model is established in the reviewed package. The proposed study should first define a measurable target, such as a terrain class or mobility-related indicator. It should assemble aligned orbital inputs and suitable reference labels, document their geographic and temporal coverage, and establish a simple baseline before adding a more complex model.

Validation should separate geographic regions so that nearby pixels from the same terrain do not appear in both training and test sets. Evaluate performance across terrain types and report error or classification metrics appropriate to the target. Compare results with the baseline and assess whether confidence estimates correspond to actual errors. Predictions on unfamiliar terrain need explicit out-of-distribution handling and may need to be withheld.

The result would be an evidence-qualified assessment, not a guarantee that a distant location is safe. Mineral identification would require suitable spectroscopic or other supporting observations, rather than visual appearance alone. Any future use of predictions inside routing must specify how uncertainty affects cost, availability and the user’s decision.

Position and environmental uncertainty

A future camera/IMU system would need localization, calibration, map registration and drift checks; an IMU alone does not establish a global Mars position. Local surface imagery and sparse rover environmental samples also do not establish current temperature or radiation at a distant site. Those capabilities require separate data and validation work.

 

10 Voice assistance and embedded development

Primary interaction concept

The future direction is a voice-assisted intelligent exploration system. A display or helmet HUD can support visual confirmation, but the proposal is not centered on a touch-operated wearable. An explorer could ask for destination evidence, request a route through the existing navigation service or dictate an observation with less manual interaction. This capability remains proposed; the current website screenshots do not demonstrate it.

The proposed processing sequence is speech capture, local speech recognition, intent interpretation, an authorized request to mission services, and a grounded spoken response. The assistant should obtain numerical answers from the route engine and scientific records rather than inventing them. Before changing a route or saving a consequential record, it should confirm the interpreted request. It should preserve corrections and indicate unavailable information.

Separation of responsibilities

The deterministic navigation service remains independent of the language model. Local maps, route calculations and records should remain usable if the voice or language-model component fails. Physical fallback controls and a concise status display can support recovery. Sensor inputs need their own quality and age indicators; an assistant’s fluent response does not validate those inputs.

A small embedded computer is proposed to run the services and store preloaded mission packs. A separate microcontroller may handle sensor acquisition or power monitoring. A Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 is a laboratory option in the team’s concept, not a finalized or space-qualified selection. Hardware choices should follow measured workloads and power/thermal limits, not an assumption that a particular board is flight-ready.

Offline operation and power

The first milestone is a complete disconnected demonstration: package all required assets, run a local route service, record observations locally and recover after restart. Later synchronization should make pending records and conflicts visible. Voice models must also be locally available if voice operation is claimed offline.

Proposed energy controls include activating speech and inference only when needed, loading only the relevant mission region, reducing unnecessary refreshes and rendering 3D on demand. Measure idle and active power, speech latency, route latency, memory, temperature and actual battery runtime. No battery-saving percentage is currently demonstrated. Holographic displays and advanced vision remain optional research; the core mission should not depend on them.

 

11 Verification and remaining work

What the current evidence supports

Source inspection supports the presence of routing, session, science and environmental modules. The supplied screenshots show mission selection, planning, comparison, simulation summary and the note-entry form. They do not prove accuracy of the underlying GIS, warning activation, successful note persistence, offline completeness or suitability for astronaut operations. This documentation does not claim a fresh test run or transfer another team’s validation results to MarsPath.

Priority completion items

Obtain original DEM, slope, CTX, SWIM and cost-raster product citations and processing histories. Verify the provisional named landmarks and LIFE_002/LIFE_003 coordinates. Reconcile older documentation with the current slope-aware balanced-route code. The current route_stats field named waypoints counts heading changes, so consumers should not interpret it as a count of science stops.

Add a contrasting-terrain route example, demonstrate the wrong-direction warning and a saved observation after reload, and test responsive and keyboard behaviour. A rover-traverse comparison could become an additional validation study, but no such MarsPath result is established here. Human mobility and spacesuit limitations would still require separate assessment.

13 Credits and evidence register

AI assistance

Team Orbit Guardians reports using OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex for code refinement, implementation, debugging, integration and documentation, and Anthropic Claude for interface redesign, restructuring and session-management code. ChatGPT/Codex also assisted preparation of this document. Team members must confirm additional tools and any earlier generated artwork before the final disclosure is submitted. No NASA logo was generated or modified for this document.

Reference document boundary

The supplied Marsline text was used only as a reference for the kind of detailed technical narrative requested. Its authors, datasets, 75 m grid, layer counts, weather-window calculations, rover-traverse validation and test statistics are not MarsPath results and are not adopted here. MarsPath’s own files and screenshots determine the claims in this document.
